output.title: Check data residency before you automate
output.body:
Before you automate a workflow, make data residency the first control, not a footnote. Residency means where the data is allowed to live and move: on your own systems, in a specific country, or inside a vendor service. For a small business, the useful question is not “can AI do this?” but “which parts of this workflow are allowed to leave my environment at all?”

Take one recurring process you already handle by hand, such as customer-data entry, invoice processing, or lead follow-up. Treat that as an illustrative workflow, not a customer case. Then list the fields that are sensitive, contract-bound, or awkward to hand to a third party: payment details, personal data, internal pricing, or anything your own service agreement says must stay in place. Bareni does not provide compliance or security guarantees; the vendor’s own documentation is where residency terms live.

The practical next step is a simple threshold check: which data fields in this workflow are required to stay in one location, and does the tool’s service agreement allow that? If most data can move, the automation path may be worth a pilot. If the data must stay local end to end, you are looking at a self-hosted or tightly integrated approach instead. That is less flashy than a demo, but it is the part that keeps Monday honest.
